newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - STN Atlas bought by Anglo-German group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - STN Atlas bought by Anglo-German group.

text.p: An Anglo-German group on Thursday signed a contract with the official receiver to buy outright STN Atlas Elektronik GmbH, a defence unit of bankrupt shipyard group Bremer Vulkan AG, for 550 million marks.

A consortium of Rheinmetall AG, Badenwerk AG and British Aerospace (BAe) beat off 30 other potential buyers in a tender process stemming from Bremer Vulkan's collapse earlier this year under a mountain of debt.
Rheinmetall will take a 26 percent stake and executive control of STN Atlas. Badenwerk will own 25 percent and BAe 49 percent, Rheinmetall chief executive Hans Brauner said.

Receiver Jobst Wellensiek narrowed down the field this week to one viable buyer, but last minute doubts over the sale arose over fears that STN Atlas -- the only profitable unit in the Bremer Vulkan group -- might be broken up.

But Brauner dismissed the speculation: "STN Atlas Elektronik should be kept in one piece. A breakup, which has been misleadingly discussed and written about, is in no way under consideration," he said.

Rheinmetall expects its STN Atlas shareholding to boost its sales next year and Brauner said the company was mulling an equity increase in 1997 to help finance his investment. He said he had also invited German companies Krauss-Maffei and Wegmann to join a holding company for STN Atlas.

The takeover, effective January 1, 1997, is still subject to the approval of German regulatory and cartel authorities. Just over half of the sale price will go towards strengthening STN Atlas' balance sheet.
Brauner said STN Atlas' Bremen operations would remain the company's main base. STN has a workforce of 4,300, of which 3,000 work in at its headquarters in northern Germany.
He added that he saw the acquisition of STN Atlas as a contribution to the consolidation process going on in the German defence industry.
STN Atlas, which specialises in marine technology, ship and system electronics and simulators, came into being as part of the Bremer Vulkan group in 1994.

The company stemmed from two firms which the German cartel wanted split off from Deutsche Aerospace back in 1989, while steel giant Krupp sold a third company, Atlas Elektronik, to Bremer Vulkan in 1991.

STN Atlas, which earned 32 million marks in profits in 1995 on turnover of 1.45 billion marks, was seen as a prize in the defence sector because it pulled in state contracts intended to put Germany at the leading edge of military technology.

Other German companies like Mannesmann, Diehl and Siemens had also expressed an interest -- and at one stage they looked to have better chances than BAe because the Defence Ministry wanted STN Atlas to stay in German hands.
The company said it expected group sales to rise by 4.8 percent to 3.6 billion marks, while order intake would jump 16.9 percent to 4.2 billion marks.
It also expected to post a 1996 net profit in double-digit millions of marks, up from six million marks last year.
